reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in education is modest and has moved down, not up. Per the Census Bureau, 30.0% of firms in Educational services (NAICS 61) answered Yes to using AI in the last two weeks, against a prior period figure of 35.5%. The Census series began asking in September 2023, and the note on the data indicates that S means suppressed, so some industry-level detail is withheld. That is the only hard adoption number in the material, and it describes firms, not classrooms or students.

What the federal government actually runs is documented in detail. The Department of Education issued AI guidance covering innovation, risk management, and an inventory of its own AI use-cases, and it says its OCIO supports adherence to federal regulations on AI advancement and responsible and secure usage, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The named tools in that inventory are CAISY, for real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation; Grammarly, for written communication feedback and language refinement; Otter.AI, for real-time transcription and collaboration; and AWS Bedrock, for building and scaling applications on foundation models. The listed uses are largely back-office and instructional support: generating summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, producing code snippets in a variety of programming languages, extracting key points and action items from public documents, generating R code for data analysis, training employees on prompt engineering, converting between related data types such as a county name and its FIPS code, generating mock data sets for testing, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, researching public articles and policies, testing filters with fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information, and suggesting descriptive paragraphs, workflow diagrams, and qualifications for public positions. This is a picture of administrative drafting and analysis, not of AI teaching students.

The vendor and money side is tracked rather than quantified here. HolonIQ describes itself as a platform for impact market intelligence, covering the global impact economy, and its stated functions are sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, scoring impact with rubrics and ratings, mapping partnership landscapes, and mapping competitive landscapes. Its stated customers are governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms, and investors, and it says global media rely on it for insight and data. The sourced points describe HolonIQ as the market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher ed, and workforce learning. No funding totals, growth rates, or market sizes appear in the excerpts, so none can be reported.

The skills and credential layer is catalogued on this site. The AI courses page lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each, and re-verified daily. The named providers are DeepLearning.AI on Coursera, Dataquest, fast.ai, DeepLearning.AI with Stanford on Coursera, Google, Hugging Face, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. Four are university graduate courses with public materials: Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191. The page states that all ten courses tracked there offer free access to core materials, though three, DeepLearning.AI's specializations and Karpathy's and fast.ai's courses, pair that with either a paid certificate option or public code repositories. It draws a distinction between university courses, generally structured around exam-driven theory, and industry courses described as code-first or hands-on, and it notes that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken. The page also states that membership is editorial, based on significance rather than sponsorship, and that nothing there is paid placement.

On risk and regulation, the material is thin but pointed. The Department of Education guidance frames permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education, per the sourced points, and the ED inventory includes a use-case for supplying fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information to ensure proper filters and data loss prevention methods are in place. That is the only explicit control-testing practice described. The excerpts do not report academic integrity policy, student-data rules, or enforcement actions, so nothing can be said about them from this material.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the sources support a narrow set of conclusions. Adoption among education firms sits at 30.0% per the Census Bureau, below the 35.5% prior period, so this is not a sector in rapid uptake by that measure. The concrete deployments documented by the Department of Education are drafting, summarization, transcription, code assistance, data conversion, and test-data generation, which are low-stakes administrative and analytical tasks with named commercial tools. The market-intelligence layer exists to size and forecast the sector, per HolonIQ, but the excerpts give no figures to act on. The training path is unusually cheap, with 11 of 13 catalogued courses free and all ten tracked courses offering free access to core materials, which lowers the cost of building internal capability. What the material does not provide is any ROI evidence, any enrollment or completion data, or any outcome measurement, so claims about learning gains or cost savings are not supported here.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
